One-paragraph summary. Two formulations are solved on the same 115 × 113 bathymetric grid, with the same mask, the same data-derived risk field R(x,y) and — for the reported L, S and J only — the same post-hoc polyline evaluator. The two optimisers are deliberately different, and integrating a route is never confused with optimising it: the grid route comes from a graph search, the spline route from a continuous SLSQP refinement, and both are then measured by the same common polyline evaluator, on their respective sampled geometries. The easy problem is an exact discrete shortest path on an 8-neighbour graph with depth and slope feasibility: Dijkstra finds the discrete optimum between selected snapped endpoint cells (173 ms repeated-solve median). Exact A/B connectors are appended and independently validated; they are not optimized over alternative connector choices. The hard problem is a cubic B-spline corridor (7 interior control points, 14 decision variables) minimising J = α·L + β·S subject to depth, slope and route-curvature constraints, solved by SLSQP from 11 distinct initial curves (14 solver executions: 11 direct and 3 quadratic-penalty continuations). The adopted point is a feasible local candidate — 2 of those executions reached feasibility, and they agree to 1 m of J — not a proven global optimum. Relative to the complete connector-inclusive grid route it changes length by -4.57 % (it is shorter, not longer) and lowers cumulative terrain risk by 26.99 %, and unlike the grid route it respects a 1350 m minimum turning radius.

1. Introduction and motivation

A tunnel between two fixed points has to be routed, not just measured. Two questions are usually conflated and are kept separate here:

  1. What is the shortest path between selected snapped endpoint cells? — a shortest-path problem on a grid, followed by validated exact-endpoint connectors. It has an exact, global answer and no notion of smoothness.
  2. What does a terrain-aware, constraint-compliant corridor cost? — a continuous optimisation problem with engineering constraints (maximum slope, minimum turning radius) and a risk penalty.

The easy problem answers (1); the hard problem answers (2). Comparing them answers the question a project actually asks: how much length do we pay for a route that respects a turning radius, and how much terrain risk do we buy with it?

Scope decisions fixed before any run (all recorded in config.yaml):

  • One risk field R(x,y) = w_s·s̃² + w_r·r̃ + w_c·c̃, weights 0.5/0.3/0.2, min–max normalisation over valid cells, no smoothing in the baseline. The weights are modeling assumptions, sensitivity-tested in Sec. 10.3 — they are not derived from, and are not validated by, the correlation analysis of Sec. 6.
  • Terrain curvature c (Laplacian of elevation) never enters route curvature; route curvature κ is never used as a terrain feature. R(x,y) is the field, S(p) = ∫ R ds is the cumulative risk along a route.
  • A third formulation was explicitly excluded by scope.

The grid is metric (metres) in both axes, so every derivative, distance and curvature below is computed without degree arithmetic. Derivatives are taken on the grid as it stands (sigma = 0 cells in the baseline), i.e. before any smoothing; the sigma-smoothing experiments in Sec. 10 re-derive everything after smoothing, which is the only way the two effects can be separated.

Resampling, masking and the domain boundary (what the code actually does). The land and NoData masks are applied to the source raster before any resampling, and the reprojection is a strict bilinear resample: a target point is accepted only when every source cell with a non-zero weight is a valid ocean cell. A land or NoData sample can therefore never be blended into an ocean value, and no value is ever extrapolated — the earlier version of this code used RegularGridInterpolator(..., fill_value=None), which extrapolates silently, and in this subset it produced 952 cells that were used as valid bathymetry although they lie outside the source footprint. The valid footprint is the cell extent of the subset (centres ± half a source cell, i.e. 11.3500–11.9000 °E × 37.0000–37.4500 °N), not the projected bounding box: projecting a lat/lon rectangle to UTM 32N gives a curved shape whose bounding box contains corners that lie outside the data. 952 of 12,995 target cells (7.33 %) are outside that footprint and are masked; a further 23 cells have a stencil that touches one of the 16 land source cells. Inside the footprint but between the outermost cell centre and the cell edge the edge cell is replicated — the half-cell border is kept rather than discarded, and no extrapolation is involved.

Derivative stencils at the array boundary. np.gradient uses one-sided differences on the outermost interior rows/columns; those cells are not excluded from the statistics or from the feasible mask, and the report says so rather than claiming an exclusion that is not implemented. The roughness window is a symmetric w × w box with mode="nearest", so at the array border the window is filled by replicating the edge cell and no artificial zeros enter the statistic. Land, NoData and outside-footprint cells hold NaN in z, so no derivative is ever taken across the mask; before a derivative stencil is evaluated, NaNs are replaced by the nearest valid ocean value (distance_transform_edt) and the result is re-masked afterwards. Feasibility is always judged on the original, unfilled arrays — the nearest-value fill exists only so that a stencil has something finite to read.

The linear striping visible in the slope map is a known signature of satellite-altimetry predicted bathymetry; it is why the TID (type-identifier) map and the σ-smoothing sensitivity are part of the analysis. Depth is d = −z with z the GEBCO elevation: d is the sea-floor depth, so d_min/d_max bound how deep the seabed is along the corridor — they are not tunnel alignment depths (Sec. 13).

3. Feature definitions

Let z(x,y) be elevation (m, negative below sea level), Δx = Δy = 450 m.

FeatureDefinitionUnits
depth d = −z m
slope s = √((∂z/∂x)² + (∂z/∂y)²), central differences (Horn/Sobel in Sec. 10) rise/run (dimensionless)
roughness r = std{s} over a 3×3 window, edges replicated rise/run
terrain curvature c = abs(∂²z/∂x² + ∂²z/∂y²), the Laplacian 1/m
normalised x̃ = (x − min)/(max − min) over valid cells, clipped to [0, 1] —
risk field R = 0.5·s̃² + 0.3·r̃ + 0.2·c̃ dimensionless, R ∈ [0, 1]
cumulative risk S(p) = ∫_p R ds (segment-midpoint rule on the route) metres

Normalisation ranges actually used (all cells, this baseline): slope 0.000–0.256, roughness 0.0000–0.0916, curvature 1.25e-09–8.04e-04 1/m.

Because min–max normalisation is recomputed for every configuration, S is not comparable across configurations (only within one). It is a length-like quantity in metres whose scale is set by each configuration's own tail; the report always says which configuration an S belongs to. The slope term is squared (s̃²) so that the field is dominated by the steepest terrain rather than by the mean.

Filling and interpolation. Land (z ≥ 0) and NoData are removed before anything else happens: they are set to NaN, excluded from the statistics, and never carry a finite value into a derivative. The hard problem needs a smooth field defined everywhere, so the masked cells are filled with the value of the nearest valid ocean cell (nearest-neighbour fill, no interpolation across the mask) and only then interpolated with a tensor-product cubic spline. The unfilled arrays are retained and every feasibility claim is checked on them (Sec. 9), so the fill can change a search field but never a validation result.

Route curvature (used only as a constraint of the hard problem): κ = (x′y″ − y′x″) / (x′² + y′²)^1.5 [1/m]; the corresponding minimum turning radius is 1/|κ|.

5. Distributions and spatial maps

Depth is a NE–SW graben flank between two shelf areas, 1.6–817 m. Slope concentrates on the flank and on the gravity-derived striping; roughness is the same structure smoothed by the local standard deviation; terrain curvature is dominated by a few sharp scarps; risk is sparse — 50 % of cells are below 0.047 while the maximum is 0.668.

The lower row is the same data after min–max normalisation: the shape is unchanged by construction (it is an affine map), which is why the histograms are shown together — it makes visible that normalisation cannot fix skewness, only re-scale it. Log-scaled counts.

The TID map shows which survey/source produced each cell. It is a data-quality indicator, not a safety map: where the striping is strongest the TID is the altimetry-predicted class, and the σ-smoothing sensitivity (Sec. 10) quantifies how much of the risk structure is that artefact.

Moran's I is computed for every feature, not only for the composite risk field, because a high I(R) could otherwise come from one feature alone:

featureMoran's I (full grid)thinned 1/2thinned 1/3cellsunit
d 0.9891 0.967 0.936 12,020 m
s 0.8965 0.736 0.619 11,568 m/m (rise/run)
r 0.8814 0.732 0.640 12,020 m/m (std of slope)

R 0.9175 0.784 0.687 11,121 dimensionless

Moran's I is reported with its cell count, its weight scheme (rook, 4-neighbour, binary) and its behaviour under thinning. No significance test is claimed: the usual normal approximation for Moran's I needs a variance derived for this weight matrix, and that approximation is not valid on a field this autocorrelated, so no z-score or p-value is quoted. The statistic is used descriptively, which is all the interpretation below needs.

Every feature is strongly autocorrelated at 450 m (I between 0.70 and 0.99), and every feature keeps most of its structure when the grid is thinned by 2 and by 3. Depth is the most autocorrelated, as expected for a smooth regional surface; terrain curvature is the least, because it is dominated by a few scarps. The thinned runs are a resolution check, not an alternative estimate: they answer "would this statistic survive a coarser survey?".

Interpretation. Slope, roughness and terrain curvature are strongly associated — Spearman is higher than Pearson because the relation is monotone, not linear. Thinning the grid by a factor of 5 in each direction (that is the factor the code uses) moves the correlations by less than 0.1, so the association is not an artefact of the 450 m sampling. Moran's I is ≈ 0.92 on the full grid and still ≈ 0.69 on a 1/3-thinned grid: the field is genuinely spatially structured, which is precisely why a route can exploit it — a random field would make routing pointless. The first PCA component of the three normalised features explains 79% of their variance, i.e. r̃ and c̃ carry largely the same signal as s̃ and the weight vector is not three independent knobs.

Association is not causation, and none of these numbers says anything about geology.

7. Easy problem

The easy problem is a minimum-cost flow / shortest-path problem on a directed graph. Write V for the feasible cells, E for the admissible edges, c_ij ≥ 0 for the metric length of an edge and b for the unit supply at A's selected snapped cell and demand at B's selected snapped cell. The route is the optimal solution of the linear program

minimise    sum_(i,j) in E  c_ij * x_ij
subject to  sum_j x_ij - sum_j x_ji  =  b_i        for every node i in V   (flow conservation)
            x_ij >= 0                                                       (non-negativity)

with b_A* = +1, b_B* = −1 and b_i = 0 otherwise, where A* and B* are the selected snapped cells. Because the constraint matrix of a shortest-path formulation is totally unimodular, the LP optimum is integral and the x_ij are the 0/1 indicator of a single path — so the LP and the discrete problem have the same answer. Dijkstra solves this LP without ever forming it: the edge weights are non-negative, so the label-setting algorithm returns the exact optimum in O(|E| log |V|). That is what makes the easy problem global: the optimum is exact by construction (Dijkstra returns the shortest path of the graph), not found by search.

Graph and feasibility definition: nodes = cells; edges = 8-neighbour; an edge exists iff both endpoints are feasible and, for a diagonal step, the geometric midpoint of the segment (bilinear interpolation of the four surrounding node samples) satisfies the depth and slope limits and all four surrounding nodes carry valid ocean data — the specification's midpoint guard, implemented in easy.midpoint_feasibility and used for the baseline. The baseline also requires both orthogonal neighbours to be feasible; reduced rules are sensitivity variants. Edge weight = metric length (450 m orthogonal, 636 m diagonal). Feasibility = not land ∧ 50 ≤ d ≤ 600 m ∧ s ≤ tan(5.5°).

8. Hard problem

8.1 Decision variables and the 14 degrees of freedom

The route is a clamped cubic B-spline p(t) = Σ N_i,3(t) P_i (i = 0…8) on a fixed knot vector, with P_0 = A and P_8 = B pinned to the endpoints and K = 7 interior control points P_1…P_7 free. Each interior control point contributes an easting and a northing, so the decision vector is

v = (u_1…u_7, w_1…w_7) ∈ [0,1]^14, P_i = origin + (u_i·W, w_i·H),

i.e. 14 degrees of freedom, box-constrained to the grid rectangle. The curve is C² by construction (a cubic B-spline is twice continuously differentiable), which is what makes a curvature constraint meaningful: κ(t) can be differentiated analytically instead of being estimated from a polyline.

8.2 Objective, constraints and how they are discretised

minimise   J(v) = α·L(v) + β·S(v),   α = 1, β = 1
           L(v) = ∫_0^1 ||p'(t)|| dt                          [m]
           S(v) = ∫_0^1 R(p(t)) ||p'(t)|| dt                   [m]   (R dimensionless)
subject to 50 ≤ d(p(t)) ≤ 600 m
           s(p(t)) ≤ tan(5.5°) = 0.0963
           |κ(t)| ≤ 7.4074e-04 1/m      (minimum turning radius 1350 m)
           κ(t) = (x'y'' − y'x'') / (x'² + y'²)^(3/2)
  • Integration and constraints. The configuration specifies n_samples = 200 and n_constraint_samples = 400, but HardProblem sets its active spline grid to the latter. Consequently the optimizer evaluates both trapezoidal L/S and collocation on the same 400 equally spaced parameter values, giving 1600 inequality rows. This describes the implemented run, not a separate 200-point objective grid. Collocation is a discretisation, so the validated route is checked separately at 2 000–5 000 points against the nominal limits; the solver targets 0.98 × the limits (a 2 % margin) so that the continuous route stays inside the nominal limits between collocation samples. The margin is a documented choice whose price is measured in Sec. 9.
  • Interpolation. d, s and R are only known on the 450 m grid, so the optimiser needs smooth surrogates. Masked cells are filled with the nearest valid ocean value and a tensor-product cubic spline (RectBivariateSpline) is fitted to each field. The cubic spline is chosen deliberately: it is the smooth field the corridor is meant to follow, its interior depth overshoot is at most 9.6 m (1.2 % of the depth range) and it never implies land (0 of 20 000 probes give d < 0, none of them on the adopted route). A bilinear (linear) interpolant has exactly zero interior overshoot, but its gradients are piecewise constant, which makes a slope constraint on a 450 m grid a different interpolation model; it is reported as a reference, not adopted. The re-solved linear-field candidate has 16 dense violations when evaluated on the baseline cubic fields; it is not treated as a validated route comparison. Along the adopted route the two interpolants differ by at most 4.9 m of depth and 0.46° of slope.

8.3 Two SLSQP strategies, and why the direct one is not enough

Direct constrained SLSQP is the literal formulation: the 1 600 collocation rows are handed to SLSQP as four vector inequalities and the method solves the corresponding NLP with its own QP subproblems. In this problem it is unreliable: with finite-difference Jacobians over 14 variables and 1 600 nearly redundant rows, the QP subproblem frequently fails along the line search. Measured here: 11 executions, 0 reaching status 0, 0 feasible.

Quadratic exterior-penalty continuation is what actually produces a feasible candidate. The constraints are moved into the objective,

φ_μ(v) = J(v) + μ · Σ_i max(g_i(v), 0)²,

and SLSQP minimises φ_μ over the 14 box constraints only, with continuation on μ = 1e2 → 1e4 → 1e6, each stage warm-started from the previous one. Measured: 3 executions from the three canonical warm starts, 3 reaching status 0, 2 feasible — both feasible runs report J within 1 m of each other, and the better of the two is the adopted route.

Three statements that matter more than the numbers:

  1. For a finite μ the minimiser of φ_μ is only approximately feasible; the penalty is exterior, so it is exactly zero on the feasible set but does not enforce it. Feasibility of the final iterate is therefore checked, not assumed (nominal limits, 2 000–5 000 points).
  2. A feasible penalty solution is not established to be a KKT point of the constrained problem: the multipliers and first-order conditions of the original constraints are not verified. Solver status is reported separately from independent feasibility, and no stationarity certificate is asserted.
  3. Feasible is not optimal. Nothing here establishes even local optimality of the constrained problem, let alone global optimality; the result is a feasible local candidate.

The solver's adopted objective is 53.259 km (trapezoidal spline integration); the hard objective evaluated post-hoc by the common polyline evaluator is 53.260 km. The difference is numerical evaluation, not a different route.

The penalty continuation is applied to the three canonical warm starts because the direct stage fails on every start; restricting it to the best direct candidates would have left no feasible result at all. Infeasible candidates have lower J than the adopted route (one of them reaches 51.844 km) precisely because they violate the slope limit — that is why they cannot be ranked against it.

8.5 What separates the hard route from the grid route

The objectives, constraints, route representation and numerical methods differ. The β sweep in Sec. 10.3 changes the risk weight while holding the hard formulation fixed and reports independently validated candidates. These comparisons illustrate sensitivity to β, but do not prove an optimal Pareto frontier or attribute the whole easy–hard length difference to any one modelling change.

8.6 Why the two objective values are not directly comparable

The easy problem minimises length subject to feasibility; the hard problem minimises length plus weighted risk subject to feasibility, curvature and its own smooth representation. Their objective functions live on different spaces (a finite graph versus a 14-dimensional continuous family), and neither feasible set contains the other: the spline family cannot represent a staircase, and the grid path is not a smooth curve. "Price of realism" and "risk reduction" are therefore comparisons of two candidate corridors under a common metric code, not differences of two optima of the same problem. Both routes are measured with the same R, the same mask and the same common polyline evaluator; the two optimisers are different by design.

β = 1, stated as a convention. L and S are both in metres, so β is a price: β = 1 means one metre of cumulative risk is worth one metre of length. The natural reference scale is β* = L_E/S_E = 17.2; at β = 1 the risk term is 4.4 % of J. The β sweep (Sec. 10.3) is the primary evidence and shows the sensitivity of these feasible candidates to β; it does not establish β-independent optimality.

9.2 Route curvature, recomputed from the B-spline itself

The optimiser evaluates κ from precomputed basis matrices. As an independent check the adopted control points are rebuilt into a fresh scipy.interpolate.BSpline object on the same knot vector, differentiated by scipy, and the curvature is formed directly from the scale formula:

The maximum observed curvature is inside the prescribed limit and the independent value agrees with the optimiser's to machine precision, so the curvature constraint is not an artefact of the solver's basis.

Two curvature estimates exist in this project and only one of them is the constraint. The optimiser constrains the B-spline, so the constraint quantity is the exact derivative-based value above — that is the number used for every feasibility statement and for the minimum turning radius in the comparison table. The smoothed-heading estimate computed on the resampled polyline (5.8158e-04 1/m, i.e. 1719 m) is a diagnostic of what a finite-difference measurement of the same curve would report; it is labelled as such everywhere and is never mixed into a feasibility verdict or compared side by side in a result table.

9.3 Continuous-domain validation against the unfilled raster

Three different notions of "inside the domain" are separated, because conflating them is how a constraint breach can hide: (i) the sample lies in a masked (land/NoData) cell, (ii) the bilinear stencil at the sample needs filled values, (iii) the interpolated depth/slope at the sample violates a limit. The adopted definition is: a point of a continuous route is continuously feasible when it is not inside a masked cell and its interpolated depth and slope satisfy the nominal limits. Results at 5 000 samples per route:

Minimum clearance to the nearest masked cell 3.6 km 3.6 km

The 27 flagged samples are explained, not waved away. Each of them lies in a 450 m cell whose node-level slope exceeds s_max, while the route point itself sits at 5.35° against the 5.5° limit — a margin of 0.15°. A node value is a cell average (and, in a difference scheme, a difference of neighbouring cell averages), so a continuous curve can clip the edge of a flagged cell while staying inside the continuous limits. No sample lies in a masked cell, none violates a limit, and the route keeps 4 km clearance from the nearest land/NoData cell, so no part of it depends on how the mask was filled.

Its solver-side collocation status alone is not a feasibility certificate, and it is not used for an improvement or validated route comparison.

The easy problem's edge rule is the specification's geometric midpoint guard. All three documented rules are solved for comparison:

Edge ruleRoute existsL_E [km]nodesnodes expandedHausdorff vs baseline [m]
node yes 53.170 94 9,618 318
midpoint yes 53.170 94 9,534 318
corner yes 53.434 95 9,530 0

The baseline rule is the combined diagonal rule: a diagonal step from (i, j) to (i ± 1, j ± 1) is admitted only when both endpoints, the geometric midpoint and both orthogonal neighbours (i ± 1, j) and (i, j ± 1) are feasible. The old corner rule checked endpoints and orthogonal neighbours but never the midpoint; the plain midpoint rule checks the midpoint and both endpoints but not the orthogonal neighbours. On this terrain the two halves of the combined rule each fail somewhere:

  • node and midpoint give the same length (53.170 km), i.e. the midpoint guard alone does not bind — a diagonal that slips past a blocked orthogonal neighbour is still admitted and is 0.264 km shorter than the baseline;
  • adding the orthogonal-neighbour condition (midpoint_corner, the baseline) rejects those diagonals and lengthens the route to 53.434 km, which coincides with the old corner result — so on this grid the neighbour half is the half that binds, and the midpoint half is the safety net that makes the rule a genuine 8-neighbour admissibility test rather than a corner-cutting check.

All four rules are reported, and only the combined one is used for the baseline. Every diagonal edge is weighted by its true length √(Δx² + Δy²) taken from the node coordinates, not by a per-axis increment, so diagonal moves are not artificially preferred or penalised.

9.6 Toy tests (seven tests, with feasibility asserted in every one)

The toy suite runs the same production functions on synthetic grids where the right answer is known analytically. Three tests on route behaviour are not enough to catch a preprocessing or validation bug, so four tests were added: the diagonal rule, the strict reprojection/masking behaviour, interpolation validity, and — the most important one — the feasibility classifier.

Toy testAssertions and outcome
T1 blocked wall route crosses the wall: True (must be False); 0 samples in blocked cells; all path nodes feasible: True; detour ratio 1.207 — the route takes a gap instead of crossing
T2 flat, zero risk L 63.957 km vs straight 63.957 km (excess 6.7e-05 %); κ_max 3.3e-05 1/m; constraints satisfied: True — with no risk to avoid, the optimum is the straight line, so the optimiser adds no gratuitous curvature
T3 single risk bump (mirrored pair) J_left 69.864 vs J_right 69.863 km (symmetry error 0.001 % ≤ 2 %); mirror error 29 m ≤ 640 m; mean risk on the route 1.78e-05 vs 0.0940 on the straight line — the route avoids the bump and the two mirrored starts find equivalent optima
T4 combined diagonal rule a step is admitted in open terrain: True; rejected when the midpoint is blocked: True; rejected when an orthogonal neighbour is infeasible: True; rejected when an endpoint is: True; cases where the midpoint binds although both diagonals' corners are feasible: 0 of 2 000 random draws — the rule is a four-condition test, not a rename of the old corner rule
T5 strict reprojection and masking open ocean accepted: True (-200 m); land-stencil point rejected: True; NoData cell rejected: True; half-cell border accepted: True; a point outside the interpolator extent but inside the source footprint is NOT silently extrapolated: True; no accepted query returned a land value: True

All seven pass (python -m src.tests_toy, exit code 0; machine-readable output in results/toy_tests.json). The suite is the argument that the numbers in Secs. 9.1–9.5 are not produced by the same bug they are meant to detect.

9.7 Runtime protocol

Five measurements are often called "the runtime". They are separated here (single machine, CPU only). Every repeated-run figure below is a median over repeated calls of the same operation on the same machine, with min–max in brackets; means are not reported because a single scheduling hiccup dominates them:

Runtime definitionValue
Easy: original baseline graph-search invocation 221.9 ms
Easy: repeated solve_easy median (includes route assembly) 173 ms (146–185 ms)

Hard: repeated penalty refinement from the adopted point 4.23 s (4.22–4.26 s)

Ratio of the two single-solve costs (median ÷ median) ×24

Basis of measurement: median of 3 repeated calls of each operation on the same machine; baseline Dijkstra timer covers graph search, while repeated easy timer covers solve_easy including route assembly; hard repetitions are penalty continuations from the adopted point.

comparison.csv names and preserves the baseline graph-search timing, original adopted penalty continuation, both repeated-run medians and the full multi-start budget separately. The graph-search single timing excludes route assembly; the repeated solve_easy timer includes it. They are distinct measurements rather than contradictory values. The full search budget is the sum of the measured solver-execution durations, not end-to-end pipeline wall time. Sensitivity CSV runtime_hard_s is the adopted continuation for that setting and runtime_multistart_s is its full search budget.

Preserved previous timing observations. Before the final reproduction run, the original baseline graph search was 173.9 ms and the repeated easy-solve median was 125 ms. The original adopted hard continuation took 6.43 s, the repeated refinement median 1.54 s, and the full 14-execution search budget 16.1 s. These are historical observations preserved in results/runtime_previous_baseline.json; the previous thread settings and machine load were not recorded, so they are not interchangeable with current-run measurements. Current values are the table above and in comparison.csv.

9.8 What is verified, and what is not

Verified by independent code: endpoints, L, S, the snapped-cell graph optimum (cross-checked against scipy), dense constraint satisfaction of both routes, continuous-domain feasibility against the unfilled raster, the curvature bound (from rebuilt spline derivatives), the interpolation comparison and all seven toy tests (including the ones that exist specifically to catch preprocessing and validation bugs: the diagonal rule, the strict reprojection, interpolation validity and the feasibility classifier). Not verified, and not claimed: global optimality of the hard route, any KKT property of the penalised solution, and any interpretation of R as a safety measure. The hard route is a feasible local candidate: only 2 of 14 solver executions reached feasibility, so the search is reported as a local candidate, not as an optimum.

10. Sensitivity experiments

Protocol: one factor at a time; for every setting both problems are re-solved, the feature stack is rebuilt, and the same metrics are recomputed by the common polyline evaluator. Budget: 3 penalty starts per run for the sensitivity sets (14 solver executions for the baseline). Everything below comes from results/sensitivity_*.csv.

Two kinds of risk column, and only one of them is comparable across settings. Min–max normalisation is recomputed inside every configuration, so S as computed within a setting (S_E, S_H) is only meaningful inside that setting. Every cross-configuration statement in this section therefore uses the frozen columns (S_E_frozen, S_H_frozen, J_*_frozen, price_of_realism_pct_frozen, risk_reduction_pct_frozen), which re-integrate the same routes against the baseline risk field — the field is held fixed, only the route changes. The baseline row is its own frozen reference, so the two column families coincide there.

Feasibility is decided by the classifier, not by the solver. A row is only marked valid_solution = True when the candidate passes the full check of Sec. 9.1 (nominal collocation, dense depth, dense slope, exact spline curvature, domain/mask, finite interpolated depth). Rows that fail keep their metrics in the CSV but are labelled INFEASIBLE and are excluded from every route-improvement claim in this section — in particular the s_max = P75 candidate is not an optimised solution, and its metrics (including the candidate S_H) are never quoted as a result.

The status column distinguishes no grid path from a path that fails independent checks. Other invalid statuses identify whether the easy path, hard candidate, or both fail. Route metrics for an invalid pair are blank. Candidate diagnostics are retained in the CSV with valid_solution = False and invalid_reason; they are not used in improvement claims.

What the column patterns say.

  • Feasibility is the fragile property, not optimality. Along the prescribed set, the settings that change the answer are the constraint and the smoothing; the settings that change the field (slope estimator, roughness window, curvature definition, κ_max) barely move the route. At s_max = P75 the feasible fraction drops to 64.8%, the feasible set shatters into 15 components and no A→B grid route exists. The smooth solver also returns an infeasible candidate; neither is presented as a valid route.
  • Slope estimator. horn changes frozen-field S_H by +0.4 % and moves the route by 73 m; sobel: grid path fails validation; the hard solver returns an infeasible candidate (feasible-cell fraction 76.3%). The estimator changes the field first and the route only second: where a feasible pair still exists the route barely moves. When independent checks fail, the candidate is not reported as feasible; this does not prove that no continuous route exists.
  • Risk is not comparable across settings when each setting's own min–max normalisation is used. Cross-setting comparisons below use the frozen baseline risk field instead.
  • κ_max barely matters: relaxing the minimum radius from 1350 m to 338 m moves the route by 62 m (Jaccard ≈ 1).
  • Roughness window changes the model. Compare resulting feasible routes using the frozen baseline field, not their separately normalised native S values.

Robustness. The two routes share the corridor loosely (Jaccard 0.11) and differ by up to 3.24 km where the grid route has to step around the flank.

Of the 37 sensitivity settings, 31 produced a candidate that passes the full feasibility check of Sec. 9.1; the rest are marked INFEASIBLE and are excluded from the statement below. On those settings, and re-integrating every route against the frozen baseline risk field so the risk numbers are comparable, the sign of both headline numbers is: the price of realism is negative in 31 of 31 settings (range -4.63 % to -3.54 %) and the risk reduction is positive in 31 of 31 (range +8.61 % to +29.75 %). Settings without a feasible A→B route (s_max = P75) remove the comparison entirely — which is itself the finding: feasibility is the fragile property, not optimality.

What the comparison does and does not claim. The hard route is a feasible local candidate under the selected model constraints, not a proven optimum of the continuous problem: 2 of 14 solver executions reached feasibility and those agree to 1 m of J, which is convergence evidence from neighbouring warm starts, not a KKT certificate. The easy graph segment is the discrete optimum between the selected snapped cells; the complete easy route includes separately appended connectors. The comparison is a statement about discretisation and representation, not about beating an optimiser: the 8-neighbour polyline is forced to zig-zag along the corridor, while the spline integrates a smooth curve through the same terrain. That is why the price of realism can be negative, and why it is reported as a length–risk trade-off rather than as an improvement.

A caveat that must travel with the headline. Part of the negative "price of realism" is discretisation, not smoothness: the easy route is measured node-to-node, and a 250 m moving-average of the same corridor is 0.56 % shorter than its discrete length (53.43 km vs 53.13 km). Even against that smoothed baseline the hard route remains shorter, but the honest statement is "the hard route is shorter than the connector-inclusive easy route by 4.6 %, of which about 0.6 percentage points are grid discretisation".

12. Interpretation: how feature-engineering choices move feasibility and optimality

  1. Feasibility is a cliff, not a slope. Moving s_max from P90 to P75 takes the feasible fraction from 77% to 65% and shatters the connected corridor into 15 components; no A→B grid route exists under this rule; this does not by itself prove that no continuous route exists. That setting is reported as infeasible everywhere in this report — including the hard-problem table, where the solver's output at P75 is not treated as a route.
  2. Smoothing is not cosmetic. σ = 2 cells changes the feasible-cell fraction to 86%, but the hard candidate fails validation, so no route metric is reported for this setting.
  3. Roughness window is a scale choice. At w = 7 the validated route moves by ~221 m; native S values on separately normalised fields are not comparable.
  4. Route curvature is imposed only on the hard problem. Slope and depth are respected by both routes; κ is constrained for the hard spline and merely diagnostic for the easy polyline. Objective and decision space differ as well, so the observed difference is not an isolated curvature cost.
  5. The risk field is a proxy. It ranks cells; it is not a geological, geotechnical or safety assessment, and no number in this report should be read as one.

13. Limitations

  • Local candidate, not a global optimum. The hard route is a feasible local candidate produced by a quadratic exterior-penalty continuation: 2 of 14 solver executions (from 11 distinct initial curves) reached feasibility, and those 2 agree to 1 m of J — agreement between two runs started from neighbouring warm starts is convergence evidence, not evidence of global optimality, and the infeasible candidates span 51.8–57.1 km, so the search landscape has many basins — we simply cannot say which of them are feasible. No global-optimality claim is made, and no KKT property of the constrained problem is established.
  • Solver fragility (accounting, not adjectives). Of 11 direct constrained executions, 0 reached status 0 and 0 were feasible on independent validation. Of 3 quadratic-exterior-penalty executions, 3 reached status 0 and 2 were feasible. The adopted candidate is slsqp_penalty from the warm_start_dijkstra_smoothed warm start; the penalty continuation is what produces a feasible route, and some sensitivity settings still return an infeasible candidate and are marked as such.
  • Two documented numerical conventions. Constraints are enforced on 400 samples with a 2 % margin and validated against the nominal limits at 2000–5000 samples. The optimizer evaluates J on 400 samples (the same active grid as the constraints). Both are choices; both are measured (Sec. 9) rather than assumed.
  • Risk is a proxy, and it is renormalised per configuration. R ranks cells by steepness, roughness and terrain curvature with weights 0.5/0.3/0.2. It is not a safety or geological measure, and S is only comparable within one configuration.
  • Depth is sea-floor depth. d_min/d_max bound the seabed depth along the corridor; they say nothing about tunnel alignment depth, cover, or overburden.
  • Data resolution. 15 arc-sec GEBCO with altimetry-predicted areas; derivatives at 450 m are at the edge of what the source supports, the striping is visible, and no independent survey validation was possible.
  • One basin, one β. The length–risk trade-off is characterised for β = 1 (with a full sweep in Sec. 10.3), on a single 50 × 51 km subset. No transferability claim.
  • Not an engineering design. No cost, no construction method, no geotechnics, no seismic or volcanic hazard, no environmental constraints.

14. Conclusion

The chain. A footprint-limited, mask-first reprojection of a GEBCO subset gives 12,020 valid cells with no extrapolation (Sec. 2–4). On that terrain the easy problem is an exact 8-neighbour shortest path between selected snapped cells, with appended validated connectors (Sec. 7), and the hard problem is a constraint-compliant cubic B-spline found by a quadratic-penalty SLSQP continuation (Sec. 8). Independent validation (Sec. 9) — a second implementation of L and S, a scipy cross-check of the search, dense continuous-domain sampling, and the exact spline curvature — cross-checks the snapped-cell graph optimum but does not establish hard-route optimality; it shows that both routes are feasible under the selected model constraints. The comparison (Sec. 11) gives L_H = 50.991 km against L_E = 53.434 km with S_H = 2269 against S_E = 3108, and the sensitivity matrix (Sec. 10) shows which of those numbers survive a change of feature engineering.

The price of realism. Read as a length–risk trade-off, the answer is a negative price: the constraint-compliant spline is 4.6 % shorter and 27.0 % lower-risk than the connector-inclusive easy route. That sign is not a claim that continuous optimisation beats graph search — the easy route is exactly optimal for its own discretisation, and part of the gap (about 0.6 percentage points) is the 8-neighbour polyline's forced zig-zag, not the constraint. The honest reading is the one the two-number summary supports: paying for realism costs smoothness and solver reliability, not length. The route that respects a 1350 m turning radius is cheaper in this terrain, and it is only available at the price of a local, multi-start, penalty-continued solve that fails outright at some settings.

What limits the answer. Feasibility depends on the chosen slope limit and on bathymetric resolution and quality; the stricter P75 setting has no grid path. The continuous solver can also fail independent validation. Risk weights are modelling assumptions and are not validated by the correlation study; no claim of general transferability is made.

Code layout.

FileContents
src/gebco_download.py GEBCO download via the public API (basket → status → zip)
src/data.py NetCDF → metric grid, reprojection, NoData/land masking, Grid
src/features.py slope (central/Horn/Sobel), roughness, terrain curvature, normalisation, risk field
src/easy.py 8-neighbour graph, geometric midpoint edge rule (+ node/corner variants), Dijkstra, exact endpoints
src/hard.py mask-aware cubic/linear interpolators + overshoot checks, B-spline path, objective, constraints, direct + quadratic-penalty SLSQP, multi-start accounting, independent curvature
src/metrics.py L, S, route curvature, dense validation, density study, domain check, Hausdorff, Jaccard
src/analysis.py descriptive stats, Pearson/Spearman, Moran's I, PCA, feasibility summary
src/pipeline.py end-to-end baseline + verification → results/baseline.json, comparison.csv
src/sensitivity.py one-factor-at-a-time experiments → results/sensitivity_*.csv
src/tests_toy.py seven toy tests (wall, flat, bump symmetry, diagonal rule, strict reprojection, interpolation validity, feasibility classifier)
src/viz.py, src/figures.py all figures
src/report.py, src/deck.py this report and the 12-slide deck

Reproduce.

python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
export OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1  # final reproduction settings
python -m src.gebco_download      # data (already cached in data/raw)
python -m src.data                # build data/processed/baseline.npz
python -m src.pipeline            # baseline + verification  (~70 s)
python -m src.tests_toy           # 7 toy tests              (~8 s)
python -m src.sensitivity --set score       # prescribed S-core experiments
python -m src.sensitivity --set full        # factor matrix
python -m src.sensitivity --set secondary   # weights, K
python -m src.sensitivity --set beta        # beta sweep
python -m src.figures             # figures/
python -m src.report              # report.md
python -m src.report_html         # report.html
python -m src.deck                # deck.pptx
python -m src.deck_preview --sheet  # one PNG per slide, for QA
python -m src.audit_submission    # final integrity checks

Environment and dependencies. Python 3.13; pinned versions in requirements.txt (numpy 2.3.5, scipy 1.17.1, pandas 2.2.3, matplotlib 3.11.2, netCDF4 1.7.5.1.post1, pyproj 3.8.0, pyyaml, python-pptx 1.0.2, Pillow, markdown). Runs on CPU only; no GPU, no proprietary data.

Dataset citation. GEBCO Compilation Group (2026). GEBCO 2026 Grid (15 arc-second global bathymetric grid). GEBCO — General Bathymetric Chart of the Oceans. doi:10.5285/4f68d5c7-45eb-f999-e063-7086abc036fa. Subset used here: 11.35–11.9° E, 37.0–37.45° N, downloaded from https://download.gebco.net (elevation and TID layers). Bathymetry in parts of the subset is predicted from satellite altimetry, not measured by multibeam sonar (Sec. 5 and Sec. 13).
